title: Chafer used Remexi malware to spy on Iran-based foreign diplomatic entities

evidences.text: This malware has previously been associated with an APT actor that Symantec calls Chafer.

The attackers rely heavily on Microsoft technologies on both the client and server sides: the Trojan uses standard Windows utilities like Microsoft Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) bitsadmin.exe to receive commands and exfiltrate data.
For more information please contact: intelreports@kaspersky.com
securelist.com /chafer-used-remexi-malware/89538 The main tool used in this campaign is an updated version of the Remexi malware, publicly reported by Symantec back in 2015.
Proliferation So far, our telemetry hasn’t provided any concrete evidence that shows us how the Remexi malware spread.

However, we think it’s worth mentioning that for one victim we found a correlation between the execution of Remexi´s main module and the execution of an AutoIt script compiled as PE, which we believe may have dropped the malware.

Malware features Remexi boasts features that allow it to gather keystrokes, take screenshots of windows of interest (as defined in its configuration), steal credentials, logons and the browser history, and execute remote commands.
Utility Usage extract.exe Deploys modules from the .cab file into the working Event Cache directory bitsadmin.exe Fetches files from the C2 server to parse and execute commands.
Send exfiltrated data taskkill.exe Ends working cycle of modules

For newer operating systems, events.exe creates task.xml as follows:

Attribution The Remexi malware has been associated with an APT actor called Chafer by Symantec.

Conclusions Activity of the Chafer APT group has been observed since at least 2015, but based on things like compilation timestamps and C&C registration, it’s possible they have been active for even longer.

Events.exe persistence records in Windows system registry keys HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Userinit HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\Microsoft Activity Manager

The malware can exfiltrate keystrokes, screenshots, browser-related data like cookies and history, decrypted when possible. The attackers rely heavily on Microsoft technologies on both the client and server sides: the Trojan uses standard Windows utilities like Microsoft Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) bitsadmin.exe to receive commands and exfiltrate data. Its C2 is based on IIS using .asp technology to handle the victims’ HTTP requests.
extract.exe Deploys modules from the .cab file into the working Event Cache directory
bitsadmin.exe Fetches files from the C2 server to parse and execute commands. Send exfiltrated data
taskkill.exe Ends working cycle of modules

Persistence modules are based on scheduled tasks and system registry. Mechanisms vary for different OS versions. In the case of old Windows versions like XP, main module events.exe runs an edited XPTask.vbs Microsoft sample script to create a weekly scheduled task for itself. For newer operating systems, events.exe creates task.xml as follows:
1 schtasks.exe /create /TN \"Events\\CacheTask_<user_name_here>" /XML \" <event_cache_dir_path>t /F"
shellexecute Silently executes received command with cmd.exe
wmic Silently executes received command with wmic.exe (for WMI commands)
Servers http://108.61.189.174 Control server HTTP URL
Main module (events.exe)
After checking that the malware is not already installed, it unpacks HCK.cab using the Microsoft standard utility expand.exe with the following arguments:
1 expand.exe -r \"<full path to HCK.cab>\" -f:* \"<event_cache_dir_path>\\\"

Exfiltration is done through the bitsadmin.exe utility. The BITS mechanism has existed since Windows XP up to the current Windows 10 versions and was developed to create download/upload jobs, mostly to update the OS itself.
